page_title: MTTR is dead, long live CIRT

sources.entry: MTTR is dead, long live CIRT

summary.name: CIRT
summary.one_liner: An opinion article proposing Critical Incident Response Time (CIRT), a metric for IT operations performance that filters to business-impacting incidents, as a replacement for mean time to resolve (MTTR).
use_cases: Choosing ops performance metrics for an on-call team
Filtering noisy alerts before measuring response time
Explaining why average resolution time can mislead
Validating whether MTTR or CIRT figures are reliable
summary.what_it_does: The article argues that MTTR averages all incidents together, mixing high- and low-urgency, manual and auto-resolved, and very short transient alerts, which skews the result. It proposes CIRT, which keeps only incidents likely to affect business: it drops low-urgency incidents, incidents not resolved by a human, incidents resolved within 120 seconds, and incidents left unacknowledged for an unusually long time. It also groups separate alerts into simulated incidents using a conservative threshold such as two minutes. The author recommends tracking the percentage of incidents acknowledged and resolved alongside CIRT to check whether the metric is meaningful.
notable: Filters incidents by urgency, human resolution, duration and grouping before computing response time
Suggests a statistically derived, customer-specific threshold for ignored incidents (e.g., two standard deviations above the mean)
Pairs the metric with the share of incidents acknowledged and resolved as a sanity check
caveats: Describes a measurement method rather than a software tool; no implementation or product is named
Thresholds such as 120 seconds and two minutes are given as examples and would need tuning per organization
